title: Iran Just Fired Missiles at US Bases in Bahrain and Kuwait. Air Raid Sirens Are Sounding Where 1.3 Million Indians Live.
excerpt: The IRGC says it struck 85 American military sites across two Gulf states. Kuwait's army is intercepting incoming drones. Oil prices are spiking. And India's massive expatriate workforce — over a million strong in these two countries alone — is caught in the crossfire of a ceasefire that may already be dead.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Iran launched missile strikes on 85 US military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait.
  • Over 1.3 million Indians live in the conflict zone, raising safety concerns.
  • Oil prices surged over 3%, impacting inflation and remittances for Indian families.
  • India's diplomatic balance is tested amid escalating US-Iran tensions.
  • Kuwait's army is actively intercepting drone attacks amid ongoing hostilities.

The fragile ceasefire between the United States and Iran is tearing apart in real time — and the fallout is landing squarely on the Gulf states where more than 1.3 million Indians live and work. For the Indian diaspora, particularly those who have built lives and careers in the Gulf, this escalation brings a heightened sense of anxiety, impacting everything from personal safety to economic stability and the ability to travel home. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps announced on Wednesday that it had launched a joint missile and drone operation against American military targets in Bahrain and Kuwait, striking what it described as 85 key US military sites. The targets included Bandar Salman and Bahrain's Fifth Naval District — home to the US Navy's Fifth Fleet headquarters — as well as Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, one of the largest American military installations in the region. Air raid sirens sounded in both countries. The Kuwaiti army confirmed it was confronting "hostile missile and drone attacks," while residents across Bahrain reported hearing explosions. The IRGC also claimed to have shot down a US MQ-9 Reaper drone attempting to interfere in the operation. The Iranian strikes came hours after the US military launched its most extensive operation since the ceasefire was signed on June 17. American forces hit more than 80 targets inside Iran, including air defence systems, coastal surveillance installations, anti-ship cruise missile sites, and more than 60 IRGC fast boats near the Strait of Hormuz. The Pentagon said the strikes were retaliation for Iranian attacks on three commercial vessels transiting the strait earlier this week — including a massive Qatari LNG tanker, the Al Rekayyat, which was hit by a drone that caused a fire in its engine room. Washington simultaneously revoked a key concession from the ceasefire agreement: a general licence that had allowed Iran to sell oil on international markets through August 21. Iran now has until July 17 to wind down all crude transactions. > **"The Kuwaiti army confirmed it was confronting "hostile missile and drone attacks," while residents across Bahrain reported hearing explosions."** ## Where India's People Are The escalation puts an enormous Indian population directly in the zone of conflict. According to India's Ministry of External Affairs, approximately 1,007,961 Indians reside in Kuwait and 332,289 in Bahrain — together roughly 1.34 million people. These are construction workers, engineers, nurses, IT professionals, bankers, and shopkeepers who form the backbone of both countries' service economies. Keralites alone account for an estimated 735,000 residents across the two nations. The safety and well-being of this significant diaspora are paramount for India, not just for humanitarian reasons but also due to the substantial remittances they send home, which are vital to many Indian families and the national economy. ![Fifth Naval District — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/9/90/Map_of_Naval_Districts_1944_Source_Furer%2C_Julius_Augustus._Administration_of_the_Navy_Department_in_World_War_II._%28Washington%2C_D.C._US_Government_Printing_Office%2C_1959%29_521..gif) India's embassy in Kuwait has said it is continuing consular services as usual amid the military escalation, though no formal advisory to Indian nationals has been issued for either country as of Wednesday morning. New Delhi's stance remains calibrated: India lodged a strong protest with the United States last month after Indian seafarers were killed in US strikes on commercial vessels in the Gulf of Oman, summoning the American Chargé d'Affaires to convey that "attacks on shipping must stop." This incident underscored the direct human cost of the conflict on Indian nationals. But the diplomatic tightrope is getting harder to walk. India needs its strategic partnership with the US. It also needs the Strait of Hormuz open — roughly 60% of India's crude oil imports transit through the waterway. And it needs its citizens in the Gulf to be safe. Historically, India has maintained a delicate balance in its relations with both the US and Iran, driven by energy needs, trade, and the welfare of its diaspora. This current crisis severely tests that balance.

## The Ceasefire Is Collapsing The memorandum of understanding signed June 17 was supposed to deliver a 60-day window for final negotiations on a permanent deal — reopening the strait, rolling back Iran's nuclear programme, and ending the broader conflict. Indirect talks in Qatar ended last week with no progress. Final-status negotiations were meant to begin after the burial of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed on February 28. His funeral procession crossed into Iraq's holy city of Najaf on Wednesday, with mourners chanting "Death to America." Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf posted on X: "The era of bullying and extortion is over. We don't fold." NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, speaking before a leaders' summit in Ankara, called the US strikes "absolutely necessary." The alliance is itself under strain, with Trump accusing European nations of failing to support the US during the Iran war. ## Markets Are Feeling It Oil prices surged more than 3% on Wednesday. Brent crude climbed to $76.56 a barrel, extending a 3% rally from the previous session. Indian stock markets opened sharply lower, with the Nifty 50 falling 0.57% and the Sensex sliding 0.47% as all 16 major sectors logged losses. The Indian rupee, which had just managed its best session in three weeks on Tuesday, is expected to weaken back toward the 95.14-95.18 range against the dollar. For the 9.4 million Indians across the Gulf — and the families in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Rajasthan who depend on their remittances — the mathematics of this escalation are brutally simple. Higher oil means higher inflation, a weaker rupee, and a more expensive life in India. This directly impacts the purchasing power of remittances sent home, making it harder for families to meet their daily needs. And now, air raid sirens in the cities they call home add a layer of existential threat to their economic worries.
